clinicalPearls: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease is the umbrella term for the pathology caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition, encompassing several distinct clinical phenotypes

Recognised phenotypes include asymptomatic chondrocalcinosis (an imaging finding), acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout), chronic CPP crystal inflammatory arthritis, and CPPD occurring alongside osteoarthritis
Chondrocalcinosis on radiographs, the linear calcification of fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage, is the imaging hallmark but is often asymptomatic

Chronic CPPD can mimic osteoarthritis, especially in atypical joints such as the wrist, metacarpophalangeal joints, and shoulder, or resemble rheumatoid arthritis with a symmetrical inflammatory pattern, so it is easily misdiagnosed
Prevalence rises steeply with age; onset in a younger patient should prompt a search for metabolic causes including haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia, and hypophosphatasia
Diagnosis rests on identifying positively birefringent rhomboid CPP crystals in synovial fluid together with supportive imaging

There is no crystal-dissolving therapy, so management targets inflammation in the acute and chronic inflammatory forms, treats any underlying metabolic disorder, and applies standard measures for associated osteoarthritis
reference.pathophysiology: CPPD disease results from excessive generation of inorganic pyrophosphate within cartilage and its combination with calcium to form calcium pyrophosphate crystals, which are deposited in fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage. Ageing cartilage and certain metabolic disturbances, such as iron overload, the hypercalcaemia of hyperparathyroidism, and low magnesium, favour crystal formation. Shedding of crystals into the joint provokes acute inflammatory attacks, while chronic deposition contributes to progressive cartilage damage and a degenerative or inflammatory arthropathy, giving rise to the range of clinical phenotypes.
additionalInvestigations: Synovial fluid polarised microscopy for positively birefringent rhomboid CPP crystals
Radiographs of the knees, wrists, and pelvis (including the symphysis pubis) for chondrocalcinosis
Ultrasound for crystal deposits within cartilage
Metabolic screen: ferritin and transferrin saturation, calcium and parathyroid hormone, magnesium, and alkaline phosphatase
Synovial fluid cell count and culture to exclude infection during flares
Cross-sectional imaging or CT where deep joints or the spine are involved
redFlags: A younger patient with chondrocalcinosis, pointing to an underlying metabolic disorder
An acute hot joint requiring exclusion of sepsis
Axial (spinal) involvement causing neurological symptoms, as in crowned dens syndrome with acute neck pain and stiffness
reference.prognosis: Outcomes vary by phenotype: asymptomatic chondrocalcinosis needs no treatment, acute attacks settle with anti-inflammatory therapy, and chronic forms may cause progressive joint damage; identifying and treating an underlying metabolic disease is important, particularly in younger patients.
pitfalls: Labelling chronic CPPD as osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis and missing the crystal diagnosis
Overlooking metabolic causes in younger patients
Assuming asymptomatic chondrocalcinosis accounts for all of a patient's joint symptoms
Forgetting that acute flares can coexist with, or closely mimic, infection
management: Aspirate the acutely inflamed joint to confirm crystals, exclude sepsis and provide symptomatic relief
Treat an acute pseudogout attack with intra-articular corticosteroid injection, an NSAID, colchicine or a short course of oral corticosteroid according to comorbidity
Use low-dose colchicine or an NSAID as prophylaxis in patients with frequently recurrent attacks
Manage chronic inflammatory CPPD with methotrexate or hydroxychloroquine where simpler measures fail
Identify and treat an underlying metabolic driver, with venesection for haemochromatosis, correction of hypomagnesaemia and treatment of primary hyperparathyroidism
Support the degenerative arthropathy with analgesia, physiotherapy and joint protection
Leave asymptomatic chondrocalcinosis untreated, reserving therapy for symptomatic disease
